pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–8 years

- **Topic:** Modelling with Sketches

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-2-ETS1-2, Engineering Design):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-2]. This performance expectation pairs SEP 2 (Developing and Using Models) with the disciplinary idea ETS1.B (Developing Possible Solutions) and the crosscutting concept Structure and Function.

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS1 Design & Technology / Working Scientifically):** Pupils generate, develop, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing and templates/mock-ups, and (in science) use observations and ideas to suggest answers — the same move of externalising a design idea as a sketch or model to show how it will work.

- **Operational details:** The child produces a sketch, drawing, or simple physical model of a solution to a given problem and — crucially — can explain how the SHAPE or structure of their design helps it do its job (a wide flat base so it won't tip; a curved roof so rain runs off; a hook shape so it can hang). The learning is the link between FORM and FUNCTION: a model is not just a picture but a way to show and think through how a design will work, and to communicate that idea to others. They relate the model back to the real-world problem it addresses, so the model is purposeful, not decorative. This sits at the 'developing possible solutions' stage of the engineering-design cycle, after defining/asking about the problem and before testing and comparing designs.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete). This is the child's first use of a model as a design-thinking and communication tool. Success = creates a sketch/model of a solution and explains how a specific shape or structural feature helps it function to solve the stated problem, connecting the model to the real problem.
bestPractices: Anchor every model to a given problem so it is a purposeful solution, not a decorative drawing.
Make the form–function link explicit: for each feature ask 'how does that shape help it work?'.
Use real objects whose shape obviously serves a function (boat hull, umbrella, spoon) as worked examples before children design their own.
Treat the sketch/model as a thinking-and-communication tool — something to show others how the design works and to improve.
Encourage labelling/annotation of features with their purpose, building explanatory vocabulary.
Allow iteration: let children change a shape and re-explain, so the model develops as their idea does.
keyRepresentations: Shape-to-function pairing (wide base → stable; sloped roof → sheds rain; point → cuts through)
Annotated sketch with feature labels explaining purpose
Real-object exemplars whose form serves a function
Design-cycle position: define → MODEL possible solution → test → compare
Model-to-problem link card (which real problem this solves)
commonMisconceptions: Treating the model as a picture to make pretty rather than a tool to show how a design works.
Not connecting the model to the problem it is meant to solve.
Being unable to say WHY a chosen shape helps the object function.
Thinking any shape will do — that form and function are unrelated.
Believing a model must look exactly like the finished object rather than illustrate the key idea.
Seeing the first sketch as final rather than something to test and improve.

learn.summary: For children aged 5–8, teach modelling as a design-thinking tool: a sketch, drawing, or physical model is a way to show and reason about HOW the shape or structure of a design helps it do its job, not a decorative picture. Anchor every model to a given problem, make the form–function link explicit ('how does that shape help it work?'), and let children iterate — change a shape, re-check, and re-explain. Use real objects whose form obviously serves a function as worked examples, and have children annotate features with their purpose.

activities.title: Shape Shop: build and test a shelter
feedback: If a flat roof lets water pool and drip through, prompt: 'What could you change about the roof shape so the water runs off instead of sitting there?'
When a child reshapes the roof into a slope and the rain runs off, affirm: 'You changed the SHAPE and that solved it — can you say why the slope helps?'
If a tower on a narrow base topples, ask: 'What shape of base would stop it wobbling?' and let them widen it and re-test.
If labels only name the goal ('stays dry'), ask them to name the feature that achieves it ('the sloped roof sends rain off the edge').
activities.rationale: Letting a child change a shape and immediately see whether it does the job makes the form–function link something they feel and can iterate on, then annotate into an explanation. An optional light physics/response check (water pooling vs running off, a wobble-test on a narrow base) and an annotate mode make the mechanism concrete; these are illustrative, not required. This supports the standard's call to develop a model illustrating how an object's shape helps it function.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-2-ETS1-2 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-2].
DfE KS1 Design & Technology requires pupils to generate, develop, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing, templates and mock-ups.
learnerActions: Read/hear the given problem: 'Design a shelter that keeps the toy animals DRY in the rain.'
Assemble a shelter from choosable parts — a base, walls, and a roof you can shape as flat, domed, or sloped — drawing or placing your solution.

Run a rain check: on a flat roof, watch whether water sits and pools (and, if the roof has gaps or leaks, drips through onto the animals); reshape the roof into a slope that overhangs the walls and run the rain again to see whether the water runs off the edge and away from the animals.
Try a stability challenge too: give a tall tower a narrow base, test it with a gentle nudge (it may wobble or topple), then widen the base and re-test to compare.
Label your finished design with why each shape helps, e.g. 'the roof is sloped so the rain runs off.'
activities.intendedInsight: It was not a fancier roof that kept the animals dry — it was the SHAPE: a slope sends water away, and a wide base helps keep a structure from tipping. Form does functional work, and a model lets you show and improve how a design works.

activities.title: Shape detectives: real objects whose shape has a job
feedback: If a child names only the object, redirect to the feature: 'Which part of the spoon lets it hold soup — what shape is it?'
Affirm form–function pairings in the child's own words: 'Yes — the hull comes to a point so it slices through the water.'
Bridge to making: 'Now you try — for your problem, what shape would do the job?'
activities.rationale: A gallery of pre-authored exemplars vividly teaches the form–function idea and builds explanatory vocabulary, priming the child to read designs. It is a reading/priming scaffold: because the examples are authored, the child does not create or adjust their own model here, so it should lead into a making activity rather than stand alone.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-2-ETS1-2 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-2].
learnerActions: Explore real objects whose shape serves a function — a boat's pointed hull, an umbrella's dome, a spoon's scoop.

For each, tap or point to the key shape-feature and reveal/say 'this shape helps because…' (the point cuts through water; the dome makes rain run off its edges, away from the person underneath; the scoop holds liquid).
Build vocabulary by naming the feature and the function it serves.
Then take your turn: pick a problem and start your own model, carrying over the 'this shape helps because…' move.
activities.intendedInsight: The shapes of made objects around us are usually chosen on purpose: the form of a designed object is tied to the function it serves, and you can read a design by asking what each shape is for.

activities.title: Design a squirrel-proof bird feeder (make-and-explain)
feedback: If the child draws a decorative, detailed picture (colours, patterns, a happy bird) with no stopping mechanism, refocus: 'Which part actually stops the squirrel? Draw just that part big.' Value the working feature over decoration.
If the model doesn't connect to the problem, ask: 'What would a squirrel try, and what about your shape stops it there?' Build the link one feature at a time.
If the child labels a wish ('no squirrels here') with no physical feature, ask: 'What SHAPE makes that happen?' and replace the label with a feature.
Probe deeper: 'Why did you make that part that shape rather than round/flat/wider?' and 'A real squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work? What would you change?'
activities.rationale: Producing and justifying one's own model is the procedural skill the standard targets; watching what a child draws and how they explain it distinguishes a functional model from a decorative picture. A making-and-talking task with raised challenges elicits independent construction and adaptation that recognition or match items cannot.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-2-ETS1-2 requires students to [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-2-ETS1-2].
DfE KS1 Design & Technology requires pupils to generate, develop, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing, templates and mock-ups.
learnerActions: Take the problem: birds keep eating from the feeder, but so do the squirrels. Design a feeder birds can use but squirrels can't reach the food in.
On paper or with simple materials, sketch or build a quick model of your idea.
Point to the specific shape or structural feature that stops the squirrels (e.g. a narrow perch, a dome, or a baffle) and explain how that feature does the job.
Relate your model back to the real feeder and the real squirrels.
Raise the challenge: a squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work? Change it and re-explain if needed.
activities.intendedInsight: A good model foregrounds the working feature and can be justified by how its shape solves the problem, and it adapts when the challenge gets harder — the model shows how a design works, not just what it looks like.

activities.title: Match the shape to its job (check of understanding)
feedback: For a correct match, prompt the reason: 'Right — why does that shape win for this job?'
For an incorrect match, point back to the function: 'What does this part need to DO? Which shape helps with that?'
activities.rationale: Image-based matching, choosing, and sorting items give a quick check of the form–function link and surface whether a child can justify a shape choice. This is an assessment/check scaffold: it does not have the child generate or refine their own model, so pair it with a making activity, which is the skill being built.
learnerActions: Look at pairs of shapes and the jobs they might do, and match each shape to the function it serves.
Given a problem, choose which of several shapes would best solve it (e.g. which roof would keep rain out).
Sort shapes into 'good for this job' and 'poor for this job' for a stated purpose, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: You can recognise which shapes suit which functions and give a shape-based reason for the match.

activities.title: Inventor coach: talk through your design
feedback: If the child restates the goal, redirect: 'That's what you want it to do — now, what SHAPE makes it happen?'
Reflect good reasoning back: 'So the wide base stops it tipping — you explained the shape AND the job.'
activities.rationale: A coaching conversation can draw out and rehearse the explanation and form–function reasoning the standard asks for. It is a support scaffold, not the lead: the modelling itself is a making/drawing act, so the conversation should react to a model the child has actually produced.
sourceClaims: DfE KS1 Design & Technology requires pupils to generate, develop, model and communicate their ideas through talking, drawing, templates and mock-ups.
learnerActions: Share a design you have already drawn or built with an 'inventor' partner (adult or in-role character).
Answer prompts: 'How does that shape help it work?' and 'Which part solves the problem?'
Explain each chosen feature and refine your words until the form–function reason is clear.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the form–function reasoning into words sharpens it and prepares you to communicate how your design works to others.

constraints: Anchor every model to a given problem so it is a purposeful solution, not a decorative drawing.
Make the form–function link explicit: for each feature ask 'how does that shape help it work?'.
Use real objects whose shape obviously serves a function (boat hull, umbrella, spoon) as worked examples before children design their own.
Treat the sketch or model as a thinking-and-communication tool — something to show others how the design works and to improve, not just a drawing.
Encourage labelling/annotation of features with their purpose to build explanatory vocabulary.
Allow iteration: let children change a shape, re-test, and re-explain so the model develops as their idea does.

Match/choose/sort items and the real-object gallery are checks or priming scaffolds — they do not elicit a child's own constructed model, which is the core skill; always pair them with a make-and-explain task.
A coaching conversation supports but cannot replace the making/drawing act; have it react to a model the child has actually produced.

A 3D builder can suit problems where three-dimensional form is the point (e.g. a stackable/stable structure), but at 5–8 it adds spatial-manipulation load; the key shape lessons at this age (stable base, sloped roof, pointed front) read clearly in 2D or on paper, so treat 3D as an optional enhancement, not the default.

Watch for misconceptions: treating the model as a picture to make pretty; not connecting it to the problem; being unable to say WHY a shape helps; thinking any shape will do; believing a model must look exactly like the finished object; seeing the first sketch as final rather than something to test and improve.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and are listed as verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims are cited to support general teaching principles (develop a model illustrating how shape aids function; model/communicate ideas through drawing and mock-ups); they do not establish the efficacy of any specific activity described here.

The original 'ideal/strong/possible' catalog rankings and claims that recognition/quiz/conversation formats 'can't' or 'trails' have been softened into scoped scaffold limits; relative-efficacy wording was not propagated as fact.

Physics responses described (water pooling/running off, a tower wobbling on a narrow base) are qualitatively reasonable for these age-appropriate examples but depend on specific setup; they are illustrative feedback mechanisms, not guaranteed outcomes of any particular implementation.

The original's explicit design-cycle positioning (define/ask → MODEL possible solution → test → compare; 'developing possible solutions' stage) is reflected only implicitly in the activities; a facilitator may wish to name this cycle stage when framing the task.

Independent re-review confirms the two previously flagged items are resolved: the 'thinking-and-communication tool' best practice is present as a constraint, and the Inventor coach activity now cites only the DfE 'talking/communicate' claim. The 'Shape detectives' gallery retains the NGSS citation on the form–function concept it teaches; reviewers should note the claim's model-development emphasis is only indirectly relevant to a read/prime activity.

probeDeeper: Show me exactly where a squirrel would try to get in — what about your design stops it there?
Why did you make that part that shape rather than round/flat/wider?
A real squirrel can jump and hang upside down — does your shape still work against that? What would you change?
assess.correctAnswer: The child produces a sketch or model whose SHAPE or structure does functional work — e.g. a narrow perch or a dome/baffle that a squirrel can't get past — and explains how that specific feature solves the problem, relating the model back to the real feeder and the squirrels.

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws a decorative, detailed picture (colours, patterns, a happy bird) rather than a model showing how the shape solves the problem.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refocus on function: 'Which part actually stops the squirrel? Draw just that big.' Value the working feature over decoration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Effort goes into appearance; no feature is identifiable as the squirrel-stopping mechanism.

errorPatterns.pattern: Model doesn't connect to the problem — the child can't say how any part of the shape keeps squirrels out.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what would a squirrel try, and what about your shape stops it?' Build the form–function link one feature at a time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked how the shape helps, gives no shape-based reason or restates the goal.

errorPatterns.pattern: Includes the goal by wishful labelling ('no squirrels here') instead of a physical feature that achieves it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Turn each wish into a mechanism: 'What SHAPE makes that happen?' Replace the label with a feature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels state the outcome but no structure in the drawing brings it about.

responseLevels.gap: Produces a decorative picture or a model with no functional feature; can't relate shape to the problem.
responseLevels.full: Produces a model whose shape does the work, explains how that specific feature solves the problem, and relates it back to the real situation — adapting it when the challenge is raised.
responseLevels.partial: Includes a plausible working feature but explains the form–function link thinly, or the model is part decoration part function without a clear mechanism.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's the problem: birds keep eating from the feeder, but so do the squirrels. Design a bird feeder that birds can use but squirrels can't reach the food in. Make a sketch or build a quick model of your idea, and show me how the shape of your design keeps the squirrels out. (Give paper/materials, set the problem, and watch what the child draws or builds and how they explain it.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching what gets drawn distinguishes a functional model from a decorative picture: a child who understands foregrounds the working feature and can point to how its shape does the job; a child who doesn't draws a pretty, detailed feeder and can't say which part stops squirrels. The link between form and function only shows in what they emphasise and explain.
